t.en: A row of stone piles. Each move merges two neighbouring piles into one, at a cost equal to their combined weight. Keep going until only one pile is left. What is the least it can cost?
Take 3, 1, 2: merge 3 and 1 first (cost 4), then with 2 (cost 6), 10 in all; or merge 1 and 2 first (cost 3), then with 3 (cost 6), 9 in all. A different order, a different cost.
An interval table again: cell (i, j) records “the least it costs to merge piles i to j into one”. A single pile needs no merging, so the diagonal is already filled with 0.

The last merge always joins one big pile on the left with one big pile on the right. Where do left and right divide? It could be any split point. Think: what does this last merge cost? And which two cells of the table hold the cost of everything before it?

This time Broom’s sweep arm works by split point: each split point sends a pair of cells, lined up as two whole runs, “left parts” and “right parts”. An Adder can add two whole runs together pair by pair.

goal.en: Each move merges two neighbouring piles, costing their combined weight. Work out the least it costs to merge a row of piles into one.

how.en: The sweep arm sends the left part and right part for every split point. The robot scans by length, shortest first, so once the circuit is built you can run it.

body.en: Each cell’s ways in are all its split points: the longer the run, the more split points. This “the last step joins two parts” structure is called interval dynamic programming.

Bracketing a chain of calculations, the best order for multiplying a chain of matrices, merging a row of neighbouring files two at a time: all of these use this kind of interval table. This board has gone into your Parts as the <part-ref to="interval"></part-ref>.

note.en: Interval merging: the last step joins a left part and a right part; pick the cheapest split point, then add the cost of the whole run.

hints.en: Look at a single split point first: before the last merge, where are the costs of merging the left part and the right part each into one pile? How should they be combined?
Pick the cheapest of all the split points (min), then add this run’s total weight.
